newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn can't use economic emergency excuse - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Bonn can't use economic emergency excuse - analyst.

text.p: Germany has no grounds for declaring an economic emergency, as the constitution requires if it wants to post a higher deficit through a supplementary 1997 budget, a prominent private economist said on Thursday.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel is widely expected to make such a declaration next week, as high unemployment and flagging tax revenues are pressuring the budget gap wider.

Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, said on Wednesday he could not exclude the possibility that the 1997 deficit would exceed government investment, which is barred by the constitution except in a critical situation.

But Horst Siebert, president of the Kiel-based Institute for the World Economy, said the economic situation did not satisfy the the constitutional conditions that would allow Bonn to declare a "disturbance of the overall economic balance".

"We have no recession, the projection for real economic growth in 1997 is about 2.6 percent. We are not threatened by recession, we forecast three percent growth in 1998," Siebert said in a television interview.
"Interest rates are low, exports are expanding, capacity utilisation is near the normal level," he added.
Article 115 of the German condition says the deficit may not exceed the level of government investment unless such an emergency is declared.
Waigel is expected to present a 1997 supplementary budget next Friday when the cabinet is due to approve his budget plan for 1998.
He said on Wednesday that Germany's current "extreme financial straits" were temporary and could be overcome through reform of the tax, pension and health-care systems.

Current planning foresees a German federal deficit of up to 56 billion marks ($31.9 billion) for 1997, already hitting the ceiling defined by government investment, but low tax revenues and high unemployment costs could add as much as 20 billion marks to that figure.
Siebert said even Germany's high unemployment was no basis for a declaration of economic imbalance, since it was a chronic situation that had been building for the past 20 years.
"If we accept high unemployment as grounds for economic imbalance, the exception clause could be used every year," he said.
